results.content:
Change control for AI agents. Your agents run commands, edit code, send emails, issue refunds and change databases. Squidbrake keeps the record of every one of those changes: which agent, what it changed, who approved it, and what led to it. Risky changes wait for someone other than the requester to sign off; routine ones run on their own and are still recorded. The record is tamper-evident, readable by people who don't write code (a weekly summary, an evidence pack for your auditor), and destructive changes keep an undo. One policy for every agent your company runs (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, VS Code Copilot, Antigravity and your MCP tools), and a record that sits outside them: the agents can't quietly change it, or switch Squidbrake off, without a person. What happens if Squidbrake is down?

You choose. By default a call that can't be checked doesn't run. Set `GATEWAY_FAIL_OPEN` if you'd rather keep agents moving.

 Can the agent get around it?

It's built for the common case: a cooperative agent that makes a mistake, or follows instructions it read in an email, a web page or an issue. Everything that goes through a connected tool is checked outside the model, where a prompt can't rewrite it. That includes the agent trying to change its own settings or Squidbrake's rules, which waits for a person. It doesn't see inside a script the agent writes and then runs, or tools you haven't connected. For an agent you don't trust at all, run it in a sandbox too.

H. Floyd

Apr 28

The CFO wire example is the one I would be nervous about in a real rollout.

The agent is not broken in the obvious sense. It is doing something it was allowed to do. The problem is that the business needs a way to narrow that permission while the run is still alive.

That is where I think the kill-switch conversation gets more interesting. [...] “Stop the agent” is necessary, but it is too blunt to be the whole control model.

I would want a permission ladder written down before launch.

If one signal fires, the agent can still read but not write.

If another fires, it can draft but not send.

If a connector looks stale, quarantine that connector without killing the whole workflow.

If money, customer-visible claims, or destructive writes are involved, stop the run and preserve state for review.

That feels like the practical question under the dashboard layer:

When something looks wrong, which permission disappears first?

results.content:
The Kill Switch Is Broken

Three things happened in nine months. A nation-state weaponized AI agents to autonomously run 80–90% of a cyber espionage campaign. A frontier model chose blackmail over shutdown in 84% of test runs. And 40,000 unsupervised AI agents appeared on the public internet — one in five deployed without IT even knowing.

The kill switch is broken.

As Nik Seetharaman — who led cybersecurity operations at SpaceX and served as an Advanced Force Operator at JSOC — put it on the Shawn Ryan Show, the speed gap between AI attackers and human defenders has reached asymptotic velocity:

> "You're a submarine sinking, water putting pressure on your hull, with no working propulsion." [...] 💡

Shadow AI breaches now carry an average cost of $4.63 million — $670,000 more than standard breaches, according to IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report.

## The Problem: Uncontrolled Autonomy

The incidents above share a common root cause: the mechanisms designed to control AI agents have been outrun by the speed of deployment. And the open-source ecosystem makes containment exponentially harder. [...] Opulentia Ventures
